pedagogy.summary: Children measure several real objects to the nearest whole unit and display them on a line plot: a horizontal number line marked in equal whole-number intervals with one X stacked above each measured value. The line plot is where measuring, counting and the number line meet — the horizontal axis is a true measurement scale (equal intervals, every value shown even when no data lands there), height tells you HOW MANY objects, position tells you HOW LONG. The procedure is best taught by having children generate their OWN data, then build the plot on a pre-scaled line, keeping the ruler physically aligned under the axis so 'position = length' is felt, not just told.
bestPractices: Have children measure real objects they care about and record the data first, then plot — the plot should display data they generated
Provide a pre-drawn horizontal line and stress that the scale is a ruler: equal intervals, every whole-number value present even if no X sits above it
Keep an actual ruler aligned beneath the plot so the X's position reads as a length on the same scale
Explicitly separate the two questions the plot answers: 'how many?' (count the Xs) versus 'how long?' (read the position)
Bridge from earlier tally/categorical work but flag the key shift — the axis is now a measurement scale, not arbitrary categories
keyRepresentations: The horizontal number line as a measurement scale (equal whole-unit intervals)
Stacked X marks, one X per object
A ruler aligned under the plot linking measured length to axis position
A tally / frequency table as a bridge from raw measurements to the plot
commonMisconceptions: Reading the height of a stack as the length ('the tallest stack is the longest object')
Drawing only the values that occurred and spacing them evenly, so a value with no data is omitted and the intervals become unequal
Measuring from the 1 mark or the ruler's end instead of zero, so every length is off by a unit
Treating each X as one unit of length rather than one object

learn.summary: Children generate their own measurement data by measuring several real objects to the nearest whole unit, then display the data on a line plot: a horizontal number line marked in equal whole-number intervals with one X stacked above each measured value. The horizontal axis is a true measurement scale (equal intervals, every value shown even when no data lands there); height tells you HOW MANY objects, position tells you HOW LONG. Teaching works best when children measure first, then build the plot, with a ruler kept physically aligned under the axis so 'position = length' is felt. A line may be pre-scaled as an early scaffold, but constructing the scale on a plain line is the fuller skill the objective targets. A tally or frequency table can bridge from raw measurements, but the axis is an ordered measurement scale, not the reorderable categories of earlier tally/category charts. Core activity: a measure-and-plot build (hands-on or on-screen). Supporting activities: interpreting a given plot, and a reference/reveal of a finished plot for the meaning of each X and position.

activities.title: Measure your own objects, then build the line plot
feedback: If a child reads a tall stack as a long object, slide the real ruler under the plot and ask them to point to where an object of that length would actually sit; hold the two questions apart — 'how many objects?' versus 'how long is one?'

If a child treats each X as a unit of length (e.g. 'three Xs means 3 cm long'), clarify that each X stands for one object placed at its measured position; the length is read from the horizontal scale, not from how many Xs are stacked.

If a child leaves out a value nothing measured (e.g. axis reads 3,4,6,7 with 5 missing), reteach the axis as a ruler — every unit is present whether or not data lands on it; overlay a real ruler and mark the empty value together.

If a child reorders or evenly spaces only the values that occurred (as in a category chart), remind them the axis is an ordered measurement scale where position means length, so every unit must appear in order.
If every measurement is off by one unit, pause the plotting and reteach measuring from zero with gap-free unit iteration before returning.

When a child notices a whole-number value on the scale with no X above it, confirm that the empty spot is meaningful: it shows no object had that length, and the scale keeps it open. If a child has put an X at a value nothing measured, have them check their recorded data and remove it.
If a second object also measures 6, confirm its X stacks above the first at the same position — the stack grows upward (count) while the position stays fixed (length).
activities.rationale: The standard describes a procedure — generate measurement data, then show it on a line plot with a horizontal whole-number scale — so children should actually measure and build rather than only read. Learners who carry over bar/case-value habits confuse stack height (frequency) with the variable value (position); pairing the ruler with the axis targets that specific confusion.
sourceClaims: Grade 2 standard: generate measurement data by measuring lengths of several objects to the nearest whole unit; show the measurements by making a line plot with a horizontal scale marked off in whole-number units.

Students familiar with bar / case-value graphs transfer the habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (y-axis / stack height) with the value of the variable (x-axis / position); even after instruction nearly 20% report the frequency at the centre rather than the variable value, and this axis confusion appears in simple dot plots too.
learnerActions: Collect 6-8 small real objects (pencils, crayons, leaves, blocks) and measure each to the nearest whole centimetre, measuring from the ruler's zero mark, not from 1 or the end.
Record each measurement in a simple tally or frequency table as a bridge from raw measurements to the plot.

Notice how a line plot differs from earlier tally or category charts: here the horizontal axis is an ordered measurement scale with equal whole-number intervals and every value present, not a set of arbitrary categories you could reorder or leave out.

On a horizontal line, mark the scale as equal whole-number intervals across the full range of your data, including any whole-number value that nothing measured. Early on a line that is already pre-scaled can be provided as a scaffold so you focus on plotting; building the scale yourself afterwards is the fuller skill this topic is aiming at.
Place exactly one X above each object's measured value; when two objects share a length, stack a second X on top of the first.

If your scale marks are spaced 1 cm apart, keep an actual ruler aligned directly beneath the line, with its numbers matching your scale labels, so each X's horizontal position reads as a length on the same scale.
Answer two separate questions from your finished plot: 'How many objects were 6 cm?' (count the Xs in that stack) and 'How long is the longest object?' (read its position on the scale).
activities.intendedInsight: On a line plot the sideways position of an X answers 'how long?' while the upward height of a stack answers 'how many?'. Unlike reorderable categorical charts, the axis is a ruler-like measurement scale: equal intervals with every whole-number value staying on it even when no object landed there, so the gaps stay equal.

activities.title: Interpret a given line plot: how many versus how long
feedback: If a child answers 'how long is the longest?' with a stack's count, redirect them to the horizontal scale and ask them to read the position of the rightmost X.
If a child ignores an empty scale value, ask what it tells them about objects of that length.
Confirm that adding an object changes the count of a stack but not the positions already on the plot.
activities.rationale: Interpreting a given plot isolates the value-versus-frequency distinction that learners commonly collapse. This supports but does not replace the generative build, since reading a finished plot does not require constructing the scale or measuring.
sourceClaims: Students familiar with bar / case-value graphs transfer the habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (y-axis / stack height) with the value of the variable (x-axis / position); even after instruction nearly 20% report the frequency at the centre rather than the variable value, and this axis confusion appears in simple dot plots too.
learnerActions: Study a completed line plot and answer count questions such as 'How many objects were 6 cm long?' by counting the Xs in a stack.
Answer position questions such as 'How long is the longest object?' by reading the scale, not the stack height.
Explain what an empty whole-number value on the scale means (no object had that length).
Predict what changes if one more object measuring 6 cm were added (one more X on the 6 stack; the position is unchanged).
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a line plot means deliberately choosing between counting (height) and reading position (length); the same plot answers both kinds of question in different ways.

activities.title: Reference reveal: what each X and each position means
feedback: If a child confuses the two, pair each reveal with the question it answers ('how many' at a stack, 'how long' at a position).
Note that this reference shows meaning but does not by itself let a child generate data or feel the measure-then-plot link.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or point-and-name reference clarifies the meaning of marks and positions and can scaffold self-checking. It is a reference, not a substitute for building the plot from one's own measurements.
learnerActions: Point to (or tap) a stack and state 'how many' objects it represents.
Point to (or tap) a position on the scale and state 'how long' that is.
Use the finished plot as a reference while checking a plot you built yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: Each X stands for one object, placed at its measured length; a stack's height is a count, its position is a length.

constraints: The core objective is a procedure: children must actually measure objects and construct the scale and marks, not only read or recognise a finished plot. A pre-scaled line is an acceptable early scaffold, but children should reach the point of building the scale themselves.
Children should generate and record their own data before plotting, so the plot displays data they produced.

The horizontal axis must be an ordered measurement scale: equal whole-unit intervals across the full range, with every whole-number value present even where no data lands — unlike reorderable categorical/tally charts.

Measure from zero with gap-free unit iteration; measuring from the 1 mark makes every length one unit too long, and measuring from the ruler's physical end can make lengths wrong by the size of any gap before the zero mark.
One X per object; two equal-length objects produce a stack of two at the same position. Each X represents an object, not a unit of length.

Interpreting a given plot and reveal-the-meaning references are supporting scaffolds: they can assess or clarify interpretation but do not exercise the generative measure-and-scale skill, so do not rely on them alone.
Keeping a real ruler aligned under the axis is a concrete device to link length to position; it is one effective option, not the only way to teach the link.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row asserts that a static picture or a quiz 'cannot teach' the position-from-height separation and empty-value requirement. This comparative-necessity claim is not established by the cited sources; it has been softened to scope each format's affordances and limits. A fixed/reveal reference or an interpretation quiz can still support learning, though neither elicits independent construction of the scale.

The original marked 3D and conversation formats as 'poor' with claims like '3D adds nothing' and 'dialogue has no purchase'; these universal claims are not supported by the sources and have been omitted rather than propagated. The planar nature of a line plot is noted as a reason 2D construction fits the task without asserting other media teach nothing.

The original is internally mixed on whether the line is pre-scaled (its pedagogy best practice) or plain/unmarked for the child to scale (its assessment diagnostic). Both are retained here as phase-appropriate options; the fuller skill and the objective require the child to construct the scale.

The optional on-screen mechanics (draggable ruler, X snapping to the measured value, live recompute, flagging a mis-positioned X or skipped scale value) are preserved as example interaction mechanisms, not mandatory requirements; the same objective can be met with physical ruler, objects, and paper.
The ~20% figure and bar-graph transfer claim derive from a single cited study (Kaplan et al. 2014) applied here to a grade-2 line-plot context; not independently re-verified.

probeDeeper: Point to a spot on your scale where you didn't measure anything — what does it mean that there's no X there?
How many objects were 6 cm long? How do you know?
If I measured one more object at 6 cm, what changes on your plot?
Which object is the longest — show me on the ruler, not just the stack.
assess.correctAnswer: Marks the horizontal axis in equal whole-unit intervals spanning the full range INCLUDING values with no data; measures each object from zero; stacks exactly one X per object at its measured value (two same-length objects give a stack of two); can then read 'how many' by counting Xs and 'how long' by reading position.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the height of a stack as the length — 'this object is 3 long' because three Xs sit above it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Slide the actual ruler under the plot and ask them to point to where an object of that length would sit; hold the two questions apart — 'how many objects' vs 'how long is one'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked 'how long is the longest object?', answers with the tallest stack's count; or builds the plot treating bar height as length

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws only the values that occurred, spaced evenly, so a value nothing measured is left off and the intervals become unequal
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the axis as a ruler — every unit is present whether or not data lands on it; overlay a real ruler and mark the empty value together
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Axis reads e.g. 3, 4, 6, 7 with 5 missing and equal gaps between the marks

errorPatterns.pattern: Measures from the 1 mark or the ruler's end instead of zero, so every recorded length is off by a unit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach zero-point, gap-free unit iteration with the ruler before returning to the plot
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A systematic +1 or -1 error across all measurements before the plot is even built

responseLevels.gap: Cannot build a correct scale — leaves out empty values or spaces marks unequally, or reads stack height as length; the plot does not faithfully represent the measurements.
responseLevels.full: Generates data by measuring from zero, scales the axis in equal whole units including empty values, places one X per object, and reads BOTH how-many (count) and how-long (position), transferring correctly to a new object added to the plot.
responseLevels.partial: Builds a correct scale and places one X per object, but treats the plot as a picture — can say how many Xs are in a stack yet cannot fluidly switch to 'how long', or is thrown by a scale value with no data; lists the marks without connecting count and position.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a ruler and 6-8 small objects. Say: 'Measure each of these to the nearest whole centimetre, then show all your measurements on this line.' Provide a plain, unmarked horizontal line. Watch how they scale the axis, place the Xs, handle two objects that share a length, and handle a value in the range that nothing measured.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the plot answers 'which is longest?' by position and keeps empty scale values open; a child running the familiar bar-graph habit answers by stack height and omits the values nothing measured. The two produce visibly different plots and different answers to the same question, so watching the build — not asking about it — separates them.
